The US official said the strikes targeted launchers that were set to fire rockets carrying mines towards the Strait of Hormuz.

Al Jazeera's Jessica Washington reports from Dhading, one of the areas worst hit by Nepal's floods, where the Trishuli River remains high and fast-moving despite receding slightly. Overnight, thick waves of mud swept through the community, destroying a funeral home and a temple, along with many homes; some buildings were reduced to bare foundations, swept entirely into the river, while others remained standing but were caked in mud inside and out.

Residents describe disbelief and uncertainty about what comes next, having lost not just their homes but their livelihoods, many having run small businesses from the ground floors of their houses. Washington says the community is in a state of shock and grief, with many convinced there are still bodies buried beneath the mud, pointing to a lingering smell of decay that can be detected on site.

Trump says Venezuelan oil will soon refill the US strategic reserve, calling it a "gift" from Venezuela and blaming Biden for draining it. 

In Washington, Al Jazeera's Mike Hanna says the reserve, now below 300 million barrels, is at its lowest since 1982, but topping it up won't be quick: the deal grants the US a 55 percent stake in heavy Venezuelan crude requiring new refineries, storage and pipelines, a process taking years, not weeks, meaning no oil reaches the reserve before the midterms. 

In Merida, independent analyst Paul Dobson says the deal has triggered backlash across Venezuela's political spectrum, effectively signing away 20 percent of its oil resources for 25 years and control over pricing and sales. Dobson argues the real winners are US corporations, not ordinary Venezuelans.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Nine years after the mass exodus of Rohingya refugees from Myanmar, more than one million stateless people remain in overcrowded camps in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar. The crisis is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain as humanitarian funding declines; refugee numbers grow and living conditions deteriorate.

In this discussion, UNHCR representative in Bangladesh, Ivo Freisen, says hope is fading as desperation grows, with about 95 percent of mainly Muslim Rohingya refugees relying fully or largely on humanitarian assistance. He warns that limited education and opportunities are pushing some young Rohingya to risk dangerous sea journeys in search of a better life.

Freijsen says a lasting solution depends on creating conditions for a safe, voluntary and sustainable return to Myanmar, including addressing discrimination, citizenship and freedom of movement.

Niger's military government says it has put down a mutiny that could have seriously threatened its rule, with loyalist forces, backed by Russian allies, retaking a military base near Niamey's international airport after hours of fighting. Officials describe the mutineers, mainly young officers from elite special forces who had travelled from the frontline regions of Tillaberi and Dosso, as rogue soldiers acting out of discontent. 

The rebellion exposed strain within an army stretched thin by fighting ISIL and al-Qaeda-linked groups on multiple fronts. Critics like Omar al-Ansari link the unrest to a shift of power toward the Presidential Guard while frontline troops are under-resourced, calling for a return to constitutional order. Pro-junta voices, including Ibrahim Boubacar, blame external enemies trying to sow division. 

Al Jazeera's Nicolas Haque reports.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
A passenger catamaran carrying 267 people capsized off the coast of Girne in Northern Cyprus, with seven people now confirmed dead, 237 rescued and 23 still missing, according to updated figures from the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus Prime Minister Unal Ustel. Al Jazeera's Resul Serdar reports the privately operated ferry left Girne around 12:30 pm local time bound for Tasucu port in Turkey's Mersin province, a busy daily route popular with tourists between Turkey and Northern Cyprus.

Eyewitnesses say the ferry began taking on water for reasons still unknown roughly five miles out, prompting the captain to turn back toward Girne. The vessel went down about 2.5 kilometres from port after the captain issued a distress call. A large search-and-rescue operation followed, involving Coast Guard vessels and helicopters, the passenger ship Akgunler, and six naval units from the Turkish Naval Forces Command, all working to locate the remaining missing passengers.

description:
In Nepal's Rasuwa district, rescuers are racing to reach more than 100 workers believed to be trapped inside hydropower tunnels sealed by mud after Wednesday's flash flood, bringing the total number of hydropower workers still missing nationwide to 933. Specialised tunnel-rescue teams from India and China have joined the operation.

The workers were at the Upper Trishuli 3A and 3B stations on the Trishuli River, connected by tunnels stretching more than seven kilometres. Heavy concrete structures shielded them from being swept away, but floodwaters packed the tunnel entrances with mud, rock and sludge, effectively sealing them shut.

Al Jazeera's Um-e-Kulsoom Shariff explains.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
In Dhading, one of the hardest-hit areas from the Nepal floods, Al Jazeera's Jessica Washington reports the overflowing river has receded slightly but remains high and fast-moving. Some homes are reduced to bare foundations, swept into the river, while others left standing are caked in mud. Many residents also lost small shops on their ground floors, telling Washington all they have left are the clothes on their backs. Some had only just rebuilt their homes after losing them in the 2015 earthquake.

In Kathmandu, Minelle Fernandez reports Nepal has asked India and China for specialist help, particularly for tunnel rescues after hydropower workers were trapped by rockfall. Authorities are reluctant to rule out the possibility of finding survivors, even as time runs short. Vehicular access to affected areas has improved from the initial helicopter-only reach, and aid, including hygiene supplies, is beginning to arrive. author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Dozens of Israeli settlers attacked a home in the West Bank village of Qusra, throwing stones as residents sheltered inside, who were then tear-gassed and detained by Israeli forces rather than protected, despite international law obligating occupying forces to do so. Homeowner Luay Bayruti says he and six others, including a worker, were handcuffed in an army vehicle for over 40 minutes and beaten. Residents say soldiers let the settlers leave, but not before they set fire to nearby land.

Three houses nearby have been besieged for weeks in what one family calls a campaign to force them out. Louai Abu Ridi says they stay up watching security cameras and are barred from seeing family, visiting the village or shopping, made worse after the military declared the area a closed military zone, trapping them with dwindling food and medicine.

title: Israeli settlers besiege Palestinian homes in the occupied West Bank
